paragraphs: So that the people would see less clearly where this arrangement led, Servius tried to give it a military look. In the second class he inserted two centuries of armorers, and in the fourth two of makers of instruments of war. In each class except the last he distinguished young from old, that is, those who were obliged to bear arms from those whose age gave them legal exemption. It was this distinction, rather than the one based on wealth, that made frequent repetition of the census, or counting, necessary. Lastly, he ordered that the assembly be held in the Campus Martius, and that all who were of age to serve come there armed.

He did not make this division of young and old in the last class as well because the common people who composed it were not granted the right to bear arms for their country. A man had to own a hearth to acquire the right to defend it. Of all the troops of beggars who today lend luster to the armies of kings, there is perhaps not one who would not have been driven with scorn out of a Roman cohort, in the days when soldiers were the defenders of liberty.

In this last class, however, _proletarians_ were distinguished from _capite censi_. The former, not quite reduced to nothing, at least gave the State citizens, and sometimes, when the need was pressing, even soldiers. Those who had nothing at all, and could be counted only by heads, were regarded as of no account whatever. Marius was the first who stooped to enroll them.

I will not decide now whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself. But I think I may assert that it could have been made workable only by the simple morals, the lack of self-interest, the liking for agriculture and the scorn for commerce and love of gain that characterized the early Romans. Where is the modern people among whom devouring greed, restlessness, intrigue, constant moving about, and perpetual changes of fortune could let such a system last twenty years without turning the State upside down? We must also note that morality and the censorship, being stronger than this institution, corrected its defects at Rome, and that a rich man found himself demoted to the class of the poor for making too much show of his riches.

From all this it is easy to understand why only five classes are almost always mentioned, though there were really six. The sixth furnished neither soldiers to the army nor votes in the Campus Martius,[1] and had almost no function in the State, so it was seldom regarded as of any account.

These were the various ways in which the Roman people was divided. Let us now see the effect on the assemblies. When lawfully summoned, these were called _comitia_. They were usually held in the public square at Rome or in the Campus Martius, and were distinguished as _Comitia Curiata, Comitia Centuriata_, and _Comitia Tributa_, according to the form in which they were convoked. The _Comitia Curiata_ were founded by Romulus, the _Centuriata_ by Servius, and the _Tributa_ by the tribunes of the people. No law received its sanction and no magistrate was elected except in the comitia. And since every citizen was enrolled in a _curia_, a century, or a tribe, it follows that no citizen was excluded from the right of voting, and that the Roman people was truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

For the comitia to be lawfully assembled, and for their acts to have the force of law, three conditions were necessary. First, the body or magistrate convoking them had to have the necessary authority. Second, the assembly had to be held on a day the law allowed. Third, the auguries had to be favorable.

The reason for the first rule needs no explanation. The second is a matter of policy. Thus the comitia could not be held on festivals or market days, when country people, coming to Rome on business, had no time to spend the day in the public square. Through the third, the senate held in check the proud and restless people and fittingly restrained the ardor of seditious tribunes, who, however, found more than one way of escaping this obstacle.

Laws and the election of rulers were not the only questions submitted to the judgment of the comitia. Since the Roman people had taken on itself the most important functions of government, it may be said that the fate of Europe was settled in its assemblies. The variety of their subjects gave rise to the various forms these assemblies took, according to the matters on which they had to decide.

To judge these various forms, it is enough to compare them. When Romulus set up the _curiæ_, he meant to check the senate by the people and the people by the senate, while keeping his own ascendancy over both. He therefore gave the people, through this assembly, all the authority of numbers, to balance the authority of power and riches, which he left to the patricians. But, in keeping with the spirit of monarchy, he still left the patricians a greater advantage, in the influence their clients had on the majority of votes. This excellent institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity, without which the patriciate, being in glaring contradiction to the republican spirit, could not have survived. Rome alone has the honor of having given the world this great example, which never led to any abuse and yet has never been followed.

The assemblies by _curiæ_ lasted under the kings until the time of Servius, and the reign of the later Tarquin was not regarded as legitimate. For these reasons royal laws were generally called _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic, the _curiæ_ were still confined to the four urban tribes and included only the common people of Rome. They suited neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, though plebeians, were at the head of the well-off citizens. They therefore fell into disrepute, and their degradation went so far that thirty lictors would assemble and do what the _Comitia Curiata_ should have done.

The division by centuries was so favorable to the aristocracy that at first it is hard to see how the senate ever failed to carry the day in the comitia that bore their name, by which the consuls, the censors and the other curule magistrates were elected. Indeed, of the one hundred and ninety-three centuries into which the six classes of the whole Roman people were divided, the first class contained ninety-eight. Since voting went solely by centuries, this class alone had a majority over all the rest. When all these centuries agreed, the remaining votes were not even taken. The decision of the smallest number passed for that of the multitude, and it may be said that in the _Comitia Centuriata_ decisions were settled far more by the depth of purses than by the number of votes.

But this extreme power was moderated in two ways. First, the tribunes as a rule, and always a great number of plebeians, belonged to the class of the rich, and so counterbalanced the influence of the patricians in the first class.

The second way was this. Instead of making the centuries vote in order throughout, which would have meant always beginning with the first, the Romans always chose one by lot, and it proceeded alone to the election. After this, all the centuries were summoned on another day according to their rank, and the same election was repeated and, as a rule, confirmed. In this way the authority of example was taken away from rank and given to the lot, on a democratic principle.
